description: Cash holding. The red colour bubbles on the network (Figure 7) show this cluster. The subject of this cluster is mainly concerned with ownership structure and cash holding. Dittmar and Mahrt-Smith (2007) documented that ineffective corporate governance spends cash quickly in ways that significantly reduce a company’s performance. The excess cash holding can be the reason for conflicts between management and shareholders. Jensen (1986) asserted that managers may have incentives to keep large cash reserves to pursue their self-interest at the expense of owners. On the other side, greater ownership by managers can align the interests of managers and shareholders (Bhagat and Bolton, 2008. Ozkan and Ozkan, 2004). Harford et al. (2008) suggested that managers must trade-off the private benefits of current expenditure against the flexibility given by cash holding. Defining agency costs in terms of asset usage, Singh and Davidson (2003) highlighted that more extensive internal ownership aligns managerial and shareholders’ interests and reduces agency costs. However, this result is not found in the case of blockholders ownership. Harford et al. (2008) illustrated how cash holdings are lower in companies with fewer shareholder rights and lower internal ownership than in companies with better shareholder rights and higher insider ownership. Similarly, Ozkan and Ozkan (2004) discussed the non-monotonic association between managerial ownership and cash holdings. Furthermore, Coles et al. (2001) and Xu et al. (1999) examined how ownership structure affects firm performance. Extended to this, Dittmar and Mahrt-Smith (2007) stated that governance raises corporate value by improving the use of cash holdings. Brown et al. (2011) did a comprehensive review and suggested that better theory is required in this subject.

Firm performance. This cluster has 32 articles. Scholars discussed agency conflicts arising from the discrepancies in the goal of large shareholders and minority shareholders. Major holding owners can be advantageous to minority shareholders, as they have the power and incentive to stop expropriation. However, large shareholders may indulge themselves in expropriating minority shareholders (Lemmon and Lins, 2003. Maury, 2006. Mitton, 2002). Fan and Wong (2005) provide evidence to reduce agency problems through the role of auditors. Scholars in this cluster have acknowledged the association of ownership structure with firm performance (Chen et al., 2005. Jara-Bertin et al., 2008. Lemmon and Lins, 2003. Maury and Pajuste, 2005. Mitton, 2002). However, researchers found inconclusive evidence of such a relationship. Douma et al. (2006) emphasised that ownership structure impacts the firm’s performance for various reasons. Firstly, owners’ differences in identity, concentration and resource endowments define their relative power, incentives and ability to control managers. Secondly, as owners have divergent goals, they impact corporate performance differently. Maury and Pajuste (2005) stated that having equal distribution of voting rights among large blockholders has a positive impact on corporate value, specifically in family-owned firms where the family is more prone to private benefit extraction if strong blockholder does not monitor them. Similarly, Joh (2003) examined the impact of ownership structure on firms’ performance before the economic crisis, whereas Lemmon and Lins (2003) and Mitton (2002) during the financial crisis. Lang et al. (2004) examined the correlation between ownership structure, analyst following, investor protection and valuation. Durnev and Kim (2005) documented that corporate with more potential for growth, more demands for outside funding and more concentrated cash flow rights engage in higher-quality governance practices which turn into greater firm value on the stock market. Furthermore, Faccio and Lang (2002) highlighted the ownership structure of Western European firms, and Morck et al. (2005) discussed the economic growth affected by the corporate sector which is generally owned by wealthy families.

Disclosure. The third cluster comprised 21 articles. The central theme of this cluster mainly focuses on disclosure, primarily affected by ownership structure within corporate governance. The ownership structure determines the extent of monitoring and, in turn, the level of disclosure (Eng and Mak, 2003). Separation of ownership from management creates agency issues. Agency theory argues that when there is greater ownership diffusion, management exploits the information asymmetry to act in a manner that is against the interest of the shareholders. To mitigate agency conflicts and information asymmetry, shareholders demand greater disclosure (Li et al., 2008. Mohd and Weetman, 2006. Donnelly and Mulcahy, 2008. Kelton and Yang, 2008). Studies concluded in this cluster that different proxies of ownership structure such as managerial ownership (Eng and Mak, 2003), foreign ownership (Barako et al., 2006. Huafang and Jianguo, 2007) and concentrated ownership (Li et al., 2008) have a positive relationship with disclosure. However, Donnelly and Mulcahy (2008) found no evidence of such a relationship. Extended to this, using the stakeholder theory method, Prado-Lorenzo et al. (2009) looked at how shareholder power and a dispersed ownership structure affected the decision to disclose corporate social responsibility (CSR). They concluded that large dominant shareholders favour social disclosure, as it ultimately relates to the long-term survival of the firm and its reputation. Similarly, Li and Zhang (2010) stated that for non-state-owned firms, corporate ownership dispersion directly relates to CSR. However, this relationship is reversible for state-owned businesses whose controlling shareholder is the state. Chen et al. (2006) investigated the impact of ownership structure in reducing financial fraud in a company.

Risk-taking in financial institutions. The cluster is the most recent among others, and the central theme of this cluster is primarily exploring the ownership structure in financial institutions. Ownership structures may affect how decisions are made and how well banks perform. Haan and Vlahu (2016) stated that ownership structures could reduce agency costs and impact the bankers’ incentives for excessive risk-taking. Laeven and Levine (2009) revealed that bank risk-taking deviates positively with the comparative power of shareholders of each bank. Similarly, Berger et al. (2016) discussed the role of ownership in a bank failure during a financial crisis. They found that significant shareholdings of lower-level management and non-chief executive officer (CEO) higher-level management are the reasons for increasing the failure risk. Furthermore, Haan and Vlahu (2016) conducted a comprehensive survey on this subject and found mixed evidence. Their study suggested that potential researchers can work on the impact of governance of large shareholders in disciplining bank management.
